question: In a child with chronic hyponatraemia, the serum sodium should not be corrected by more than 10–12 mmol/L in any 24-hour period, to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is true and describes a critical safety principle. Over-rapid sodium correction in chronic hyponatraemia causes osmotic demyelination syndrome. The maximum safe correction rate is 10–12 mmol/L per 24 hours. In contrast, acute symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, coma) may require urgent small boluses of 3% saline (1–2 mL/kg) to raise sodium by 5 mmol/L acutely, but controlled correction must then continue slowly.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia (particularly correction >12 mmol/L/24h) risks osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS, formerly central pontine myelinolysis). The brain adapts to low osmolarity over time; abrupt restoration of osmolarity causes demyelination. Correction should generally not exceed 10 mmol/L/24h in high-risk patients and 12 mmol/L/24h in others.
